Oh, constantly. I mean... that's exactly it. That's actually the whole reason I finally made the appointment to come in here and talk to someone. I just... I keep beating myself up, day in and day out, over this idea that I’m not really senior material. 

Like, I got this senior analyst title a while back, right? And I only have a high school diploma. But instead of feeling good about it, I just have this overwhelming, sickening sense that I fooled everyone. I really feel like I completely tricked the IT director, the whole management team, everyone... I fooled them all into thinking I could handle way more than I actually can. 

And now I’m just waiting for the other shoe to drop. Every time I send an email, every time I submit a report on system performance or network latency, I’m obsessing over what they’re thinking when they read it. I picture them sitting in their offices, looking at my work, and just realizing, 'Wow, this guy has no idea what he's doing.' It’s exhausting. I'll spend three hours drafting a five-minute update for the morning stand-up meeting because I'm so terrified I'll use the wrong terminology and expose myself as a complete fraud. 

I just keep beating myself up over it, constantly telling myself I don't belong at this level, that I took a job I have no business doing and that I'm letting everyone down by pretending I can do it. Even when I'm driving home, I'll replay conversations I had with the developers, analyzing every word I said, worrying that I sounded stupid. So, yeah, I worry about their opinions non-stop. It's the main reason I'm sitting in this chair right now, honestly, because I just can't take the constant feeling that I'm pulling a fast one on the whole company and that they're all about to figure it out.

Well, it's funny you ask that, because I've been trying to pinpoint exactly when this whole... this whole cycle really kicked into high gear. I mean, I've always had a little bit of imposter syndrome, I think most people in tech do, especially when you don't have the formal education to back it up. And the director called me into his office, and I thought I was in trouble, honestly. I thought I'd messed up a server migration or something. But instead, he asked me to step up and cover the senior analyst duties until they could find a replacement. 

And at first, I was like, 'Wow, okay, they trust me.' But almost immediately, within days of taking on that workload, that's when the bottom fell out. That's when I started looking at the network architecture diagrams and the high-level strategy documents Mark left behind and thinking, 'I have no idea what I'm looking at.' I mean, I do, technically, but I convinced myself I didn't. And that's when the guilt started, this idea that I had somehow tricked the director into thinking I was capable of filling Mark's shoes. So, yeah, it was about a month ago, right when I got handed those senior duties, that this whole rollercoaster really took off and I started feeling like the biggest fraud in the building.

I'm still doing the actual mechanics of the job just fine, it's just the mental gymnastics afterward that are wearing me out.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself engaging in all-or-nothing thinking, where you believe you're either completely competent or a total failure, with no middle ground?\n\nPatient: All-or-nothing... like, black and white? I mean, I didn't go to college, sure, but I've been in the trenches of IT for over twenty years. And that gap, that space between the six and the nine, that's where all this guilt is living. That's where the imposter feeling comes from. \n\nSo I guess, to answer your question, no, I don't have that all-or-nothing thing going on. I'm actually painfully aware of the middle ground. I just feel like I'm tricking people about exactly where I sit on it, if that makes sense.\n\nDoctor: Are you feeling like you're able to hide these feelings of guilt and inadequacy from your coworkers, or are they starting to notice a change in you?\n\nPatient: Well, I... It's not like we're all sitting around a big conference table pitching marketing ideas and chatting all day. A lot of the time, I've got my noise-canceling headphones on, I'm staring at two, sometimes three monitors, and the only communication I have with the guy sitting in the cubicle literally three feet away from me is through Microsoft Teams. We just ping each other. So in that sense, it's pretty easy to just put your head down and pretend everything is fine. I just type my status updates, send my reports, and keep my mouth shut.
